chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from one who informed him from Ibn Tayfur the physician, who said:

Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) asked me, 'What do you ride?' I said, 'A donkey.' He asked, 'For how much did you buy it?' I said, 'For thirteen dinars.' He said, 'This is extravagance (saraf): that you buy a donkey for thirteen dinars and leave aside a thoroughbred horse.' I said, 'O my master, the maintenance of the thoroughbred is more than the maintenance of the donkey.' He said, 'Indeed, the one who maintains the donkey is the one who maintains the thoroughbred.'

Do you not know that whoever ties up a beast, expecting through it our affair, and irritates with it our enemy, and it is attributed to us, may God increase his provision, broaden his chest, fulfill his hope, and be a help to him in his needs?

key_terms.أَمْرَنَا: Our affair (referring to the Imam's cause or religious duty)
key_terms.اِرْتَبَطَ دَابَّةً: To tie up/keep a beast (for use)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on the cost of maintaining horses for religious purposes?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) redefines the concept of 'usury' (saraf) not merely as a financial transaction but as a missed spiritual opportunity, arguing that the high maintenance cost of a horse is justified by its role in 'waiting for our affair' (intizar al-faraj) and jihad. He emphasizes that equipping oneself with a noble mount, dedicated to the Imam's cause, invites divine expansion of the heart and sustenance, transforming material expenditure into an act of worship. This reflects the Shia scholarly view that material resources are instruments for spiritual and political readiness, where the value lies in the intention and status of the asset rather than its mere utility.
